## The problem

Our team of twelve engineers has drifted into long-lived feature branches that survive for weeks, sometimes months. Merges have become dreaded events rather than routine ones. Last quarter's payments-refactor branch took three days to integrate and broke checkout in staging for two more. This isn't a one-off: it's the predictable result of letting code diverge for long stretches before anyone reconciles it.

- Merge conflicts compound with time and branch age, so the longer we wait, the more painful and risky integration becomes.

The cost isn't just engineering time. It's delayed feedback: bugs and design mismatches surface weeks after the decisions that caused them, when they're expensive to unwind. It's also a morale problem — nobody enjoys a merge day that feels like defusing a bomb.

## The proposal

I'm proposing we move to trunk-based development: all engineers commit small, frequent changes directly to main (or through very short-lived branches, under a day), gated by feature flags for anything incomplete, and backed by a CI suite that runs on every commit.

- Feature flags let us ship incomplete work safely, decoupling deployment from release.
- Small, frequent commits mean code review happens on diffs of tens of lines instead of thousands, catching problems while they're still cheap to fix.

This isn't a radical experiment — it's standard practice at Google, Facebook, and most high-performing engineering organizations, and it pairs naturally with our existing CI investment.

## What could go wrong

The strongest objection is real: trunk-based development demands strong CI discipline and comprehensive automated tests, and our current suite has gaps, particularly around integration tests for the billing service. If we adopt this workflow before shoring up coverage, we risk shipping broken code straight to main instead of catching it in an isolated branch. I take this seriously — it means our rollout should start with a two-week investment in test coverage for the riskiest modules, not a flip of the switch tomorrow.

- We should also expect a short adjustment period as people build new habits around flagging and smaller PRs; that's a one-time cost, not a permanent one.

I would like a decision by the end of next week.
